'''Hannah Marion Critchlow''' (born 1980) is a British scientist, writer and broadcaster. Her academic research has focused on cellular and [[molecular neuroscience]].<ref>{{cite book |last= Critchlow |first= Hannah |title= Consciousness |publisher= [[Ladybird Books]] |location= London, England |date=2018 |isbn= 978-0-7181-8911-2 |others=illus. Stephen Player }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Critchlow|first1 = Hannah M|last2 = Herrington|first2 = Paul|last3 = Gunton|first3 = Simon|date = 1 Feb 2012|title = Inside an unquiet mind: Music and science join forces to explore mental ill health|journal = EMBO Reports|volume = 13|issue = 2|pages = 95–99|doi = 10.1038/embor.2011.255|pmid = 22240971|pmc = 3271342}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Critchlow|first1 = HM|last2 = Maycox|first2 = PR|last3 = Skepper|first3 = JN|last4 = Krylova|first4 = O|date = 2006|title = Clozapine and haloperidol differentially regulate dendritic spine formation and synaptogenesis in rat hippocampal neurons|journal = Molecular and Cellular Neuroscience|volume = 32|issue = 4|pages = 356–365|doi = 10.1016/j.mcn.2006.05.007|pmid = 16844384|s2cid = 33783762}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1 = Critchlow|first1 = HM|last2 = Payne|first2 = A|last3 = Griffin|first3 = DK|date = 2006|title = Clozapine and haloperidol differentially regulate dendritic spine formation and synaptogenesis in rat hippocampal neurons|journal = Cytogenetic and Genome Research|volume = 105|issue = 1|pages = 4–10|doi = 10.1159/000078002|pmid = 15218251|s2cid = 46245478}}</ref> In 2014 the [[Science Council]] named her as one of the ten leading "communicator scientists" in the UK.<ref name=TimesHE20140117/> In 2019 ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' listed her as one of Cambridge Universities "Rising Stars in Biological Sciences".<ref name=Nature2019d41586-019-01925-w/> In 2022 she was awarded an Honorary Doctorate from [[Brunel University of London|Brunel University]] for her work in neuroscience and communication.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's happening at Winter grads |url=https://students.brunel.ac.uk/campus-news/whats-happening-at-winter-grads |access-date=2023-04-15 |website=students.brunel.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> In 2026 she is due to receive the [[Rosalind Franklin Medal]] from the Humanist Society. 

==Early life and education==

Critchlow decided on a career in neuroscience as a teenager after working as a nursing assistant at [[St Andrew's Hospital]].<ref name=Neuroscience/><ref name=Telegraph20150627/><ref name=Guardian20180518/> She studied Cell and Molecular Biology at [[Brunel University London|Brunel University]],<ref name=Telegraph20150627/><ref name=Guardian20180518/> where she was awarded a First Class degree in 2003 along with three undergraduate University Prizes.<ref name=Magdalene/> While studying at Brunel she had secured a work placement from [[GlaxoSmithKline]], who with the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] provided a CASE Award for her doctoral<ref name=PhD-612238>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=https://copac.jisc.ac.uk/id/35561324?style=html|title=The role of dendritic spine plasticity in schizophrenia|first= Hannah Marion|last=Critchlow|date=2008|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.612238}}|website=jisc.ac.uk|oclc=890154350}}</ref> studies at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name=Telegraph20150627/><ref name=Magdalene/>

==Career and research==

Following completion of her PhD, Critchlow spent a year as a Kingsley Bye-Fellow at [[Magdalene College, Cambridge]]<ref name=Magdalene/> and then a further year as a researcher at the Institute for the Future of the Mind,<ref name=Magdalene/> funded by the [[Oxford Martin School]] at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=IftFotM/> In 2008 she returned to [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge]], where she has been professionally based ever since, apart from a one-year secondment to the [[British Neuroscience Association]] in 2010–2011.<ref name=Magdalene/><ref name=Neuroscience/>

In parallel with her research career, Critchlow began to establish herself as an effective science communicator and public face of science. She took part in a Rising Stars programme run by the [[University of Cambridge]]'s Public Engagement team in 2011<ref name=BustingBrainMyths/> and, together with the cosmologist Andrew Pontzen, produced a series of Naked Shorts on their research for the award-winning podcast ''[[The Naked Scientists]]''.<ref name=Magdalene/><ref name=BustingBrainMyths/> A series of talks developed by Critchlow to take to schools and public festivals led to her giving a talk on "brain myths" at the [[Hay Literary Festival]] in 2015 that attracted national and international media interest.<ref name=Telegraph20150525/><ref name=Metro20150526/><ref name=NYT20150602/> This led in turn to her being commissioned by [[Penguin Books]] to write an introductory book on Consciousness<ref name=PenguinBooks/> and to presenting Tomorrow's World Live for the BBC<ref name=TWL/> and Family Brain Games.<ref name=FBG/> In 2017 Critchlow was appointed as a Science Outreach Fellow by [[Magdalene College, Cambridge]]<ref name=Magdalene/><ref name=Neuroscience/><ref name=PenguinBooks/> She was a judge for the 2018 [[Wellcome Book Prize]].<ref name=WellcomeBookPrize/> In 2019 she was elected member of the prestigious European Dana Alliance of the Brain and named by Nature as one of Cambridge University's 'Rising Stars in Life Sciences' <ref name=Nature2019d41586-019-01925-w/> in recognition for her achievements in science engagement. That same year her second book was published called [[The Science of Fate]] and made it onto the Sunday Times Bestseller list.<ref name=TheTimes2019may-19-xqs5zc3xk/> Her third book [[Joined up Thinking]] was published in 2022 to critical acclaim.
